sections.h2: Which Trenton offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
Billing, valuing and appeals sit in three different places. The Division of Tax sends bills and takes payments, the Tax Assessor puts a value on each parcel, and the Mercer County Board of Taxation hears disputes. City guidance tells taxpayers that questions about a valuation belong with the assessor.

  • Division of Tax (billing, payments, delinquent notices, the annual tax sale): 609-989-3070.
  • Tax Assessor (value, deductions, exemptions, appeal forms): 609-989-3083.
  • Mercer County Board of Taxation, McDade Administration Building, 640 South Broad Street, Room 317, Trenton: 609-989-6704.

The Division of Tax also keeps records and files the reports state law requires, and it prepares lists of properties for tax foreclosure.

sections.h2: Who owns homes in Trenton, and what does that mean for a sale?
sections.html:
Mostly renters, in a compact capital city. Trenton is the capital of New Jersey and the seat of Mercer County, and it served briefly as the capital of the United States, from November 1 to December 24, 1784. Its motto, "Trenton Makes, The World Takes," dates from an industrial past of iron, steel, rubber and pottery, though today the state government dominates the local economy.

The Census Bureau counted 90,871 residents in 2020 and estimates 91,506 for 2025, packed into 7.58 square miles of land. That works out to nearly 12,000 people per square mile. Trenton is the only New Jersey city served by three commuter rail systems, Amtrak, NJ Transit and SEPTA, and the Trenton Transit Center sits in the East Ward beside Trenton Central High School.

Wikipedia describes the East Ward as the smallest of the city's neighborhoods and the West Ward as home to its more suburban streets, with Downtown, Hanover/Academy and Mill Hill among the named areas. Value and housing type shift a good deal from one part of the city to the next, so a figure for Trenton as a whole is only a starting point.

A seller here is often dealing with a rowhouse or older single family home on a small lot, sometimes with a tenant inside. The Census shows why: only 37.9% of homes are owner-occupied.

sections.h2: What is Trenton's tax calendar and mailing pattern?
sections.html:
Installments fall on the first day of four months: February, May, August and November. Ten days of grace follow each one before a balance turns delinquent. Trenton does not follow the July mailing pattern used by calendar year towns. The city mails bills twice a year.

  • Late June or early July: bills for the August and November quarters.
  • Late December or early January: bills for the February and May quarters.

The first-half bills are the preliminary ones, based on about half of the prior year's taxes. When the second-half bill is issued it uses the current year's rate, and the preliminary amount is subtracted from the full-year total. That is why the winter quarters can look different from the summer ones even when the assessment has not moved.

sections.h2: What does a late Trenton payment cost?
sections.html:
Delinquent balances accrue 8% a year up to $1,500 and 18% beyond that, measured from the opening day of the quarter once grace runs out. The city points to N.J.S.A. 54:4-67 for those rates. Once a delinquency has used up the $1,500 tier, later delinquencies are charged at 18% until the account balance returns to zero.

A 6% penalty may also be added to a delinquency above $10,000 that is still open at the end of the fiscal year. Partial payments are accepted under the same interest terms. For a receipt, mail a stamped return envelope with the stub; otherwise the canceled check serves as proof.

sections.h2: When can Trenton sell a lien on unpaid taxes?
sections.html:
A municipal tax bill or charge still unpaid on May 11 is open to the tax sale, provided the sale takes place before the fiscal year ends on June 30. The city cites N.J.S.A. 54:5-19. From May 11 until the sale, payments must be made by certified check, cash or money order.

The rule is the same every year, and the Division of Tax holds the sale annually. An owner who plans to sell with taxes behind should clear the balance or have the payoff figure ready before May 11, because a lien adds a separate redemption step to the closing.

sections.h2: Where does a Trenton owner file an assessment appeal?
sections.html:
Each year, April 1 closes the window for ordinary appeals and December 1 closes it for added or omitted assessments. Both go to the Mercer County Board of Taxation. If your assessment exceeds $1,000,000 you may file directly with the New Jersey Tax Court, and a decision from the county board can be taken to Tax Court within 45 days.

Under Mercer County's instructions, a copy of the petition is served on the board at 640 South Broad Street, and the municipal assessor and municipal clerk each get one too. The board does not accept faxes or emailed copies. Its appeal page also offers an appeal checklist, appeal reminders and a comparable sales analysis form, and a seller who has recent sale prices for similar homes nearby should attach them. The county's 2026 notice put the deadline at Wednesday, April 1, 2026, which has passed, so a new filing now would be for the next tax year. The state Division of Taxation adds that the owner carries the burden of showing the assessment is out of line with market value.

sections.h2: How should the bill change hands when a Trenton house sells?
sections.html:
Pass the bill to the buyer. City guidance says a bill belongs with the new owner after a sale, and a fee may apply to a duplicate. Before the closing date, ask the Division of Tax what is paid and what is open, since delinquency interest runs back to the start of the quarter.

Flood zone status is another item the city mentions: if your municipality qualifies for federal flood insurance, an owner who does not buy it can be denied federal disaster assistance. Information on whether a property lies in a flood zone comes from the Municipal Clerk, which is worth checking when you list a home near the Delaware River.

faqs.q: What number reaches Trenton's tax staff?
faqs.a: Call the Division of Tax at 609-989-3070. Assessment and deduction questions go to the Assessor at 609-989-3083. The collection office does not answer value questions.

faqs.q: What is the grace period for Trenton property tax?
faqs.a: Ten days after the first of February, May, August or November. After that, taxes are delinquent and interest is counted from the first day of the quarter.

faqs.q: When is the Trenton tax appeal deadline?
faqs.a: April 1 for ordinary assessments and December 1 for added or omitted ones. The Mercer County Board of Taxation takes the filing, and an assessment above $1,000,000 can go straight to Tax Court.

faqs.q: Why do my first-half and second-half Trenton bills differ?
faqs.a: The winter bill is a preliminary figure near half of last year's taxes. The summer bill applies the new rate for the year and subtracts the preliminary amount already billed.

faqs.q: Can Trenton sell a lien if I have owed tax for a long time?
faqs.a: Yes. A bill unpaid on May 11 can be sold, provided the sale happens before June 30. After May 11 the city takes only certified funds, cash or a money order.
